scenes.visual: Title card: More species, more biomass. Use grassland silhouettes; introduce the broader ecosystem-function story.

scenes.tts: Grassland experiments give a clear result. Plots with more plant species generally grow more aboveground biomass. Losing species can therefore change what an ecosystem does: how much plant material it produces. Richer communities also tend to have steadier total production from year to year. At Cedar Creek in Minnesota, the total became steadier even though individual species became less stable. The important result is about the whole community, and how its different species work together.

scenes.visual: Show species-poor and species-rich experimental grassland plots, then harvested aboveground biomass. Label the general pattern: more plant species, generally more biomass. Use schematic comparisons without numerical axes or invented measurements. Transition to community production across years, with proportionally less variation in the richer community; individual species can still fluctuate.

scenes.tts: Why can a mixture produce more? Complementarity means species, on average, do better together than their monocultures predict. They may use resources differently, or help one another. Legumes adding nitrogen are one example. Selection is another explanation. A richer random draw is more likely to include a highly productive species that dominates. Both can act together. The Loreau and Hector partition separates complementarity and selection in the yields. But the partition alone does not identify the biological mechanism.

scenes.visual: Two panels: complementary resource use and legumes adding nitrogen; then a randomly assembled community containing a productive species that dominates. Join the panels with net effect = complementarity + selection. Label the partition as yield accounting and show that identifying a biological mechanism requires more than the partition.

scenes.tts: Now ask what steadier means. Temporal stability is mean total biomass across years divided by its standard deviation. If species fluctuate independently, their ups and downs partly cancel in the total. A higher mean production can also raise stability. Resistance means how little production changes during a disturbance. Resilience means how fully or quickly it returns afterwards. Grassland experiments found greater resistance to wet and dry climate events, but no detectable diversity effect on recovery one year later.

scenes.visual: Display temporal stability = mean / standard deviation beside community biomass through time. Use schematic independent species fluctuations and their sum, without implying that species must move in opposite directions. Then show disturbance and recovery as separate stages: greater resistance in the grassland synthesis, no detectable diversity effect on recovery one year later.

scenes.tts: How do we know richness matters? At Cedar Creek, researchers sowed randomly chosen species with the same seed mass in every plot. They clipped, dried and weighed the plants each year. Random composition prevents researchers from simply choosing productive species for richer plots. BIODEPTH repeated the logic across eight European grassland sites. Across those sites, losing plant species reduced average aboveground biomass.

scenes.visual: Animate random draws from a species pool into plots with different richness and equal total seed mass. Show clip, dry, weigh. Connect Cedar Creek in Minnesota to eight European BIODEPTH sites. End on the observed overall decline in average aboveground biomass with species loss; do not imply every individual plot or site responded identically.

scenes.tts: Real landscapes add a complication. Wetter or more fertile soil could support both more species and more biomass. Field studies found positive biodiversity and biomass associations after adjusting for environmental differences. But an unmeasured variable could still drive both. Experiments assign richness. Surveys need that extra caution.

scenes.visual: Show soil moisture and fertility pointing to both richness and biomass. Contrast randomly assigned experimental richness with observational field associations adjusted for environmental differences. Keep a possible unmeasured confounder visible; do not label the field association as proof of causation.

scenes.tts: One smaller point: the benchmark matters. A mixture can beat the average monoculture without beating the best. Extra yield against the average does not mean it outproduces every species grown alone.

scenes.visual: Closing card labelled Smaller point: the benchmark. Show a schematic mixture above the average monoculture but level with the best. Label average and best; use no numerical yields.
End card: Biodiversity and ecosystem function. Echo the richer grassland and biomass motif.
